This EPA is partially a reflection of your own performance in the case and partially a reflection of your ability to coach your junior resident in performing most of the case. For your own parts of the case, to get to the next level as you perform more of these operations, you’ll develop your own moves to facilitate your efficiency and effectiveness. I think some of those moves could include dissecting the critical view of safety by starting as close to the wall of the cystic duct and artery as possible, and then after creating those windows clearing the remaining fibroadipose tissue bluntly towards the common duct towards the liver to avoid evulsion injury of critical structures. Once the gallbladder has been removed from the cystic plate, getting it out of the body cavity can facilitate exposure. Exposure of the cystic plate for hemorrhage control can also be facilitated by using the surgeons left working hand to hold up segment 4B of the liver down to the caudate lobe, and the retraction port instrument to push down on the viscera. For taking your Junior through the case, I think the most important advice you should reiterate is more active use of their left hand to facilitate exposure and tension on the tissues, which will make the right hand much more effective. If they aren’t ready to be active with both hands, it is probably best to give them only their right hand. There is certainly value in letting someone struggle through a case, but taking over earlier can be merciful if they are not being safe or not making progress, and there were times during this case when not much progress was being made and we should have taken over to show some moves and then give it back. Overall, you did well, and this was a very good learning case with an excellent result of a safe and effective operation and the patient going home without complication the next day.

This was a lap chole being performed for gallbladder polyp without significant inflammation. Performance was between direct and indirect supervision. Dr. ***** clearly understands the steps of the operation and was able to identify the cystic artery, cystic duct, and other anatomical structures but did require significant input to fluidly progress through the case as well as minor assistance/change over by the chief resident for a small duration of the procedure. I think with continued repetition he will progress towards indirect supervision quickly. General principles I would encourage (for everyone) in dissection of the hepatocystic triangle include very selective/limited use of cautery, starting high on the gallbladder and using Maryland forceps with the “tips up” to clear any fatty/fibrous tissue overlying the duct and artery, using the left hand to provide dynamic retraction of the infundibulum, and really clearing the bottom third of the gallbladder from the hepatic fossa to achieve the critical view. Also, I would encourage open communication with the person running the camera when transitioning from the anterior and posterior view of the gallbladder. *** demonstrated careful tissue handling but my only slight criticism would be to make smaller more frequent “spreads” around the duct/artery as opposed to large spreads until the anatomy can be more reliably delineated. He did shine on dissecting the GB from the hepatic fossa, recognizing areas of tension, adjusting his exposure to provide additional tension, and not getting into the thin-walled gallbladder! Overall he did a very nice job!

Teaching points:  to do open preperitoneal hernia repair you make a standard hernia incision, find anterior rects sheath and incise the anterior fascia to the rectus edge and then put a finger under all the layers lateral to rectus and divide.  The gets you to the preperitoneal plane.  Sweep the peritoneum off the abdominal wall bluntly and find tge tubercle and coopers.  Divide epigastrics, and the identity hernia.  You frequently need to open the hernia neck to reduce, medial for femoral and direct, lateral for indirect.  If concerned open pertoneum to inspect contents.  Ligate the sac and suture mesh to coopers, anterior abdominal wall and upper facia for you entrance incicision and then close
